sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Eventual consistency is the guarantee that, given no new writes, all replicas of a piece of data will eventually converge to the same value — trading strong read-freshness for high availability and low latency, at the cost of requiring conflict-resolution strategies such as **last-writer-wins (LWW)**, **vector clocks**, and **CRDTs**.

Eventual consistency is the weakest useful consistency guarantee in the distributed-systems spectrum: it promises only that, if you stop writing and wait long enough, every replica will return the same value. During the convergence window — typically milliseconds within a datacenter, seconds across regions, minutes across the global DNS — reads can return any value the local replica has ever observed, including stale, conflicting, or intermediate values. This sounds dangerous, and it would be if applied indiscriminately to billing or inventory. But for the vast majority of user-facing workloads — social feeds, recommendation counts, profile photos, comment threads, search indexes, DNS records — a few seconds of staleness is invisible to the user, and the latency and availability gains are enormous. Amazon's Dynamo paper (DeCandia et al., 2007) introduced eventual consistency as a first-class engineering choice, and the systems that descended from it (Cassandra, Riak, Voldemort, DynamoDB's eventual reads) now run a large fraction of the planet's user-facing traffic.

The motivation is mechanical. A strongly consistent store must reach quorum on every write, which means at least one round-trip to the slowest quorum member; this caps write throughput at the leader's append-fsync rate and adds the cross-DC RTT for geo-replicated data. An eventually-consistent store can accept writes at any replica, propagate asynchronously, and serve reads from the nearest replica — sub-millisecond p99 reads, horizontal write scalability, and full availability during partitions. The cost is that two replicas may simultaneously accept conflicting writes (the same key updated by two clients in different regions), and the system must converge them to a single value when the replicas exchange state. The choice of convergence strategy is the central design decision.

**Last-writer-wins (LWW)** is the simplest: each write carries a timestamp, and the write with the highest timestamp wins. LWW is what Cassandra uses by default, what DynamoDB uses for `consistentRead=false` writes, and what DNS uses for SOA record updates. Its advantage is simplicity — no application code, no conflict detection, deterministic resolution. Its disadvantage is that it silently drops data on conflict: if two clients both update the same shopping cart item, the later one wins and the earlier one is lost. LWW also requires tightly synchronized clocks; a 200ms NTP skew between two datacenters can flip the winner and corrupt data. **Vector clocks** (Lamport, Mattern, Fidge, 1988–1991) detect concurrency rather than resolve it: each write carries a vector of per-node logical counters, and the system can determine whether two writes are causally ordered (one supersedes the other) or concurrent (both must be presented to the application). Riak and Voldemort use vector clocks; the application receives siblings and must merge them. The advantage is correctness — no silent data loss — but the cost is application complexity and the risk of sibling explosion on hot keys.

**CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)** (Shapiro et al., 2011) are data structures whose merge operation is associative, commutative, and idempotent, so any two replicas that have received the same set of updates — in any order — converge to the same state without coordination. Counters (G-Counter, PN-Counter), sets (G-Set, 2P-Set, OR-Set), and sequence CRDTs (RGA, LSEQ) are the building blocks. CRDTs are what make collaborative editors (Yjs, Automerge) and DynamoDB's counter type work; Riak has a CRDT library built in. The advantage is automatic, deterministic convergence without application conflict resolution; the cost is that CRDTs are domain-specific (you cannot make arbitrary data structures conflict-free) and that some operations (like "delete then re-add") require tombstones that grow unboundedly without periodic compaction. **Read-repair** is the propagation strategy: when a coordinator reads from multiple replicas and sees divergence, it writes the converged value back to the lagging replicas — fixing divergence as a side effect of reads. **Anti-entropy** is the background strategy: replicas periodically exchange Merkle trees of their key ranges and sync any differences; Cassandra's `nodetool repair` and Riak's `active anti-entropy` are examples. **Hinted handoff** handles temporary unavailability: if a replica is down, the coordinator stashes the write on another node with a hint to forward it when the original replica returns.

Real-world systems illustrate the trade-offs. **Amazon DynamoDB** with `consistentRead=false` provides single-digit-millisecond reads at scale; the same table can be read with `consistentRead=true` at twice the cost when needed. **Apache Cassandra** at `ONE`/`ONE` provides sub-millisecond reads and is the substrate for Instagram's feed metadata, Netflix's playback history, and Apple's sizeable user-data store. **DNS** is the original eventually-consistent system: zone updates propagate via SOA serial numbers and TTL-driven cache expiry, accepting minutes-to-hours of staleness in exchange for the resilience that has kept DNS running through every major internet incident since 1985. **Redis Cluster** uses eventual consistency for cross-slot reads during failover, with a brief window where the new primary may not have all writes from the old one. **Amazon S3** provides read-after-write consistency for new objects (since 2020) but historically was eventually consistent for overwrites, a constraint that shaped how Netflix and Airbnb designed their asset pipelines.

The architect's rule of thumb is to default to eventual consistency for any workload where (a) the user is not the only writer (so read-your-writes is not strictly required), (b) the data is derived from other authoritative sources (so it can be rebuilt), or (c) the cost of a stale read is less than the cost of a refused write. Inventory counts, account balances, transaction ledgers, and lock ownership must be strongly consistent. Profile fields, comment counts, social graphs, recommendation features, search indexes, and analytics dashboards should be eventually consistent. The middle ground — read-your-writes session consistency — covers most user-facing apps where a user must see their own writes immediately but other users' staleness is invisible. Eventual consistency is not "no consistency"; it is "consistency with a budget," and the budget is a design parameter you choose per feature.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as Client A (us-east)
    participant C2 as Client B (europe)
    participant R1 as Replica 1 (us-east)
    participant R2 as Replica 2 (europe)
    C1->>R1: write(x=1, ts=100)
    C2->>R2: write(x=2, ts=200)
    Note over R1,R2: concurrent writes (no causal order)
    R1->>R2: anti-entropy (Merkle tree compare)
    R2->>R1: divergence detected
    Note over R1,R2: LWW: x=2 wins (ts=200 > 100)
    R1->>R1: apply x=2 (read-repair)
    R2->>R2: confirm x=2 (already local)
    Note over R1,R2: CONVERGED
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   us-east replica                europe replica
   +-------------+                +-------------+
   |  x=1 ts=100 |   partition   |  x=2 ts=200 |
   |  (write A)  |   - - - - - - |  (write B)  |
   +------+------+                +------+------+
          |                              |
          |  anti-entropy exchange       |
          +----------> Merkle <----------+
                      compare
                      |
                      v
        LWW resolution: x=2 wins (higher ts)
                      |
                      v
   +-------------+                +-------------+
   |  x=2 ts=200 |  <-- read-repair --> | x=2 ts=200 |
   +-------------+                +-------------+
                  CONVERGED (no new writes)
```

### Walkthrough
1. Two clients concurrently write to different replicas during a network partition.
2. Each replica accepts the write locally (high availability, no quorum needed).
3. The partition heals; anti-entropy compares Merkle trees and detects divergence.
4. LWW resolution picks the write with the higher timestamp (x=2).
5. Read-repair writes the converged value back to the lagging replica; future reads are consistent.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Eventual-consistency simulator with LWW and vector-clock conflict detection.
import threading, time

class Replica:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.data = {}                       # key -> (value, ts, vector_clock)
        self.vc = {self.name: 0}             # this replica's vector clock
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def write(self, key, value, ts):
        with self.lock:
            self.vc[self.name] = self.vc.get(self.name, 0) + 1
            self.data[key] = (value, ts, dict(self.vc))

    def read(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            return self.data.get(key, (None, 0, {}))

    def sync_with(self, other):
        """Anti-entropy: pull other's state, apply LWW or detect siblings."""
        with other.lock:
            other_snapshot = dict(other.data)
        with self.lock:
            for key, (val, ts, vc) in other_snapshot.items():
                local = self.data.get(key)
                if local is None:
                    self.data[key] = (val, ts, dict(vc))
                    continue
                local_val, local_ts, local_vc = local
                if _concurrent(local_vc, vc):           # vector clock says concurrent
                    print(f"[{self.name}] CONFLICT on '{key}': "
                          f"{local_val} (ts={local_ts}) vs {val} (ts={ts}) "
                          f"-> LWW picks ts={max(local_ts, ts)}")
                if ts > local_ts:                       # LWW
                    self.data[key] = (val, ts, dict(vc))

def _concurrent(vc1, vc2):
    """Two vector clocks are concurrent iff neither dominates the other."""
    dominates_1 = any(vc1.get(k, 0) > vc2.get(k, 0) for k in vc1)
    dominates_2 = any(vc2.get(k, 0) > vc1.get(k, 0) for k in vc2)
    return dominates_1 and dominates_2

# Simulate two replicas accepting concurrent writes during a partition.
r1 = Replica("us-east")
r2 = Replica("europe")
r1.write("cart", ["apple"],   ts=100)
r2.write("cart", ["banana"],  ts=200)        # concurrent write, partitioned
print("before sync  r1:", r1.read("cart"))
print("before sync  r2:", r2.read("cart"))
r1.sync_with(r2)                              # anti-entropy triggers LWW
print("after  sync  r1:", r1.read("cart"))   # converges to banana (ts=200)
print("after  sync  r2:", r2.read("cart"))   # still banana (local winner)
```

quiz.explanation: Eventual consistency is the guarantee that if no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses will return the last written value. The liveness property is convergence: in a system where replicas communicate reliably and infinitely often, all replicas reach the same final state.

quiz.explanation: A vector clock is a map from node-id to logical counter, maintained per replica. When a replica performs a local write, it increments its own counter in the vector. When it sends a message, it attaches its current vector; the receiver takes the per-component max of its own vector and the incoming vector, then increments its own counter.

quiz.explanation: Read-repair propagates divergence lazily during reads: the coordinator reads from multiple replicas, detects divergence, and writes the converged value back to lagging replicas. It is cheap (no background work) and self-correcting for hot keys, but cold keys can diverge indefinitely.
